content: WD repeat-containing protein 3 (WDR3) is a protein encoded by the WDR3 gene in humans. This gene produces a nuclear protein that contains 10 WD repeats. WD repeats are structural motifs consisting of approximately 30 to 40 amino acids, characterized by several conserved residues, typically including a tryptophan-aspartic acid (Trp-Asp) sequence at the C-terminal end. Proteins that belong to the WD repeat family are implicated in a wide range of cellular functions, such as cell cycle regulation, signal transduction, programmed cell death (apoptosis), and the regulation of gene expression. To investigate the function of WDR3, model organisms have been utilized. Specifically, a conditional knockout mouse line, named Wdr3tm1a(KOMP)Wtsi, was developed as part of the International Knockout Mouse Consortium program. This program is a large-scale mutagenesis initiative aimed at creating and distributing animal models of human diseases for research purposes. Both male and female mice from this knockout line underwent a standardized series of phenotypic tests to assess the consequences of WDR3 gene deletion. A total of 24 tests were conducted on the mutant mice, and two significant abnormalities were identified. Notably, no homozygous mutant embryos were detected during gestation, indicating that these embryos did not survive to the weaning stage. The remaining tests were performed on heterozygous mutant adult mice, but no additional significant abnormalities were observed in these animals.
